title: Pholiota and historical Pholiota names in southwest Michigan

scope.basis: All 1,317 GBIF occurrence results returned for Pholiota in Michigan were checked for these county labels, yielding 25 specimens; iNaturalist Research Grade species counts for these nine counties returned 10 Pholiota names. Coordinates without county labels were not assigned to counties here.
scope.limitations: This is complete for the retrieved, scoped records after stated grouping and exclusions, not an exhaustive biological census. Native status is not independently established by occurrence records. Historical determinations have not been re-examined.

additions.name: Golden scalycap group
additions.aliases: golden Pholiota, golden scalycap, chestnut mushroom, Pholiota adiposa group, Pholiota aurivella, Pholiota limonella, Pholiota cerifera, Pholiota connata, Pholiota squarrosoadiposa, Pholiota squarroso-adiposa
additions.months: Mainly summer–fall; a local May collection is also on record
additions.habitat: Clusters on hardwood logs, stumps and standing deadwood; sometimes conifer wood
additions.id: Sticky yellow to orange caps with brownish scales, attached gills turning brown, and a brown spore print.
additions.look: Shaggy and sharp-scaly Pholiota, honey mushrooms and Gymnopilus. Honey mushrooms have white spores, but a spore print alone does not establish identity.
details: Caps are often 2.5–12 cm across, with scales that can wash off or disappear into the slime. Stems are comparatively dry, with scales and a fragile ring zone.
Names in this complex overlap. Cap color and a photograph cannot reliably separate aurivella, limonella and adiposa; microscopic and molecular interpretation may be needed.
additions.taxonNote: One aggregate entry covers the adiposa / aurivella / limonella complex. Historical connata and squarrosoadiposa records are cross-referenced here, not counted as additional confirmed species.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Sharp-scaly Pholiota
additions.aliases: sharp scaly pholiota, sharp-scaly pholiota, scalycap, Pholiota squarrosoides
additions.habitat: Clusters on decaying hardwood logs and stumps
additions.id: Whitish cap beneath pointed tawny scales; cap can be sticky between scales; gills change from pale to rusty brown.
additions.look: Toxic shaggy scalycap (Pholiota squarrosa) can be extremely similar. Weather affects stickiness and older gills lose useful color clues.
details: Caps are usually 3–11 cm wide; the stem has tawny scales and a short-lived ring zone. The spore print is cinnamon brown.
Microscopy may be needed: published descriptions distinguish its small, poreless spores from the larger spores of P. squarrosa. Do not decide food safety from cap stickiness.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Shaggy scalycap
additions.aliases: shaggy Pholiota, scaly Pholiota, shaggy scalycap, Pholiota squarrosa
additions.habitat: Dense clusters at hardwood bases, roots and stumps; sometimes conifers
additions.id: Dry yellowish cap and stem with prominent upturned brown scales; mature gills and spore print are brown.
additions.look: Sharp-scaly Pholiota has overlapping features and can require microscopic separation. Honey mushrooms can share the clustered habit.
details: A shaggy partial veil leaves a ring or ring zone. Some collections have a garlic-like odor, but odor is variable.
Michigan State University considers this species poisonous. Do not eat it; avoiding alcohol does not make it safe.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Flaming scalycap
additions.aliases: flaming Pholiota, flame scalycap, Pholiota flammans
additions.habitat: Dead conifer logs and stumps, singly or in clusters
additions.id: Fresh caps and stems are bright yellow with equally yellow shaggy scales; mature gills become cinnamon brown.
additions.look: Golden scalycaps usually have contrasting brown scales. Old or rain-damaged fruit bodies lose the distinctive bright-yellow appearance.
details: The cap is commonly 4–8 cm wide and may be slimy beneath its yellow scales. A yellow veil leaves a ring zone on the stem.
Check the wood type, young scales, attached gills and brown spore print together. Worn specimens may need microscopy.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Multicolored Pholiota
additions.aliases: multicolored scalycap, multicolour Pholiota, Pholiota polychroa, Pholiota ornella, Pholiota appendiculata
additions.habitat: Hardwood logs, stumps and fallen limbs; occasionally conifers or sawdust
additions.id: Slimy caps can mix olive, green, purple-gray and yellow-orange; a pale veil may leave patches at the margin.
additions.look: Other slimy Pholiota and blue-green Stropharia can overlap in appearance. Green or purple coloring does not indicate psychoactivity or food safety.
details: Caps are variable in size and color, often losing green and purple shades as yellow tones develop. The stem may retain patches of veil below a fading ring.
The spore deposit is principally brown; the original description notes a slight purplish cast when moist. Confirm anatomy rather than relying on color alone.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Slender Pholiota group
additions.aliases: slender scalycap, Pholiota spumosa, spumosa complex
additions.habitat: Decayed wood, buried wood, sawdust and forest litter, often with conifers
additions.id: Smooth sticky yellow-brown caps with a darker center; yellowish gills become cinnamon brown and stems darken from the base.
additions.look: Several small yellow-brown Pholiota, including P. prolixa, overlap. Toxic sulfur tufts and deadly Galerina must also be excluded.
details: Caps are often 3–6 cm wide and can have olive tones. Veil remnants are usually fibrillose rather than a durable skirt.
Treated as a field group because the traditional spumosa complex contains similar taxa. Species-level determinations usually require microscopic characters.
additions.taxonNote: The local community records use P. spumosa; this card retains a broad field-group interpretation.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pale sticky Pholiota
additions.aliases: pale scalycap, sticky scalycap, Pholiota lenta, Flammula lenta
additions.habitat: Humus, woody debris and soil rich in decaying litter
additions.id: Pale cream to buff, very sticky caps with scattered white veil remnants; pale gills turn grayish brown.
additions.look: P. lutescens and other pale Pholiota are similar. Deadly small brown mushrooms can lose or gain apparent color with age and weather.
details: Caps may reach 3–10 cm across. The white stem often browns at the base and carries a fragile veil zone rather than a lasting ring.
Small smooth spores and cystidia are important for separation. Retain substrate and fresh specimens for expert examination.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Granular Pholiota
additions.aliases: granular scalycap, Pholiota granulosa, Flammula granulosa
additions.habitat: Wood and debris of hardwoods or conifers
additions.id: Small dry amber-brown caps with tiny granular scales over a yellow background; yellow gills and a slender darkening stem.
additions.look: Small Flammulaster and other granular brown mushrooms can be very similar. Macroscopic characters alone may not resolve them.
details: Caps are commonly 1–3.5 cm wide. Fine yellow veil remnants may hang from the margin and remain on the thin stem.
The original treatment emphasizes confusion with other small scaly species. Microscopy is needed for a reliable determination.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota angustipes
additions.aliases: narrow-stemmed Pholiota, Hypodendrum angustipes, Pholiota angustipes
additions.habitat: Soil in grassy ground or near stumps and buried woody material
additions.id: Brown caps fade toward tan and carry tiny dotlike scales; the stem can taper downward and the ring is fleeting.
additions.look: Agrocybe, other brown Pholiota and deadly small brown gilled mushrooms require expert separation.
details: The historical treatment describes caps 2–8 cm across with only slight stickiness when wet. Attached pale gills mature to cinnamon brown.
Dotlike cap scales are useful but may be absent on some caps. Confirm spores, cystidia and substrate; the local occurrence is a community identification.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Burn-site Pholiota group
additions.aliases: bonfire scalycap, charcoal Pholiota, Pholiota highlandensis, Pholiota carbonaria, Flammula carbonaria
additions.months: Spring–fall; a local December specimen is also on record
additions.habitat: Burned ground, charred wood and buried wood at fire sites
additions.id: Clusters of small slimy reddish-brown to orange-brown caps with pale margins, attached brown-maturing gills and a veil zone.
additions.look: Other burn-site Pholiota are difficult to separate. Deadly Galerina and other brown-spored wood fungi remain important comparisons.
details: Caps are often 2–6 cm across. Pale veil remnants may form patches or scaly bands below the stem apex.
This is a species-group entry: the old carbonaria label and closely similar burn-site taxa require taxonomic interpretation, not identification from a photo.
additions.taxonNote: The Barry County specimen was catalogued as Flammula carbonaria. This historical name is cross-referenced under the highlandensis group.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Yellowing Pholiota
additions.aliases: Pholiota lutescens, yellowing scalycap, Pholiota lutescens var. fallax
additions.habitat: Hardwood stumps and soil mixed with woody debris
additions.id: Pale to whitish sticky caps, gills and flesh develop yellow tones with age; veil remnants can be sparse.
additions.look: Pale sticky Pholiota (P. lenta) and other yellow-brown Pholiota overlap; a historical variety label complicates the local record.
details: The typical published form has caps about 2–7 cm wide, attached gills and a fibrillose stem that can narrow below.
The local herbarium record includes the determination “var. fallax.” The specimen has not been re-examined for this guide, so its modern species interpretation remains provisional.
additions.taxonNote: Historical local specimen, not a new verified determination; see the original variety remark in the source checklist.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota malicola
additions.aliases: forgettable Pholiota, Flammula malicola, Pholiota malicola, malicola group
additions.habitat: Clusters at trees and stumps, on woody debris or from buried wood
additions.id: Yellow to orange-yellow caps become smoother as they age; gills turn rusty brown and a pale veil leaves a weak ring zone.
additions.look: Flammula alnicola and related smooth yellow wood fungi are difficult to separate. Sulfur tufts and Gymnopilus also need exclusion.
details: Caps can begin conical and become broadly umbonate. The yellowish stem typically darkens toward the base.
Authorities differ on boundaries in the malicola / alnicola complex. No tasting is suggested for identification; microscopic work is needed.
additions.taxonNote: Retained under the name used by the local specimen and Species Fungorum; other taxonomic treatments place it in the Flammula alnicola complex.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota paludosella
additions.aliases: bog Pholiota, Naucoria paludosella, Pholiota paludosella
additions.months: Local June record; September–October in the species treatment
additions.id: Cream-colored sticky caps with a tawny scaly center; yellowish gills become cinnamon brown and the stem darkens below.
additions.look: Other bog-dwelling Pholiota and Galerina can closely resemble it. Bog habitat alone is not diagnostic.
details: The monograph describes caps usually 3–5 cm across with buff veil remnants and a fibrillose ring zone.
Spore and cystidial measurements are needed for confident separation from P. sphagnicola and related fungi. No verified example photo is supplied here.
additions.taxonNote: The Berrien County specimen was collected on Sphagnum at Mud Lake Bog and catalogued as Naucoria paludosella.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota parvula
additions.id: Tiny sticky tawny caps, pale gills that become cinnamon brown, and a slender yellowish stem that darkens at its base.
additions.look: Other small Pholiota, Galerina and Hypholoma cannot be excluded from cap color and size alone.
details: Caps are typically only 1–2 cm wide; the cobwebby yellow veil is easily lost. The stem tapers downward.
Microscopic spores and chrysocystidia are essential to distinguish this obscure species. Warren Woods specimens support a historical local record.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota prolixa
additions.habitat: Clusters around stumps and buried wood in low, wet hardwood woods
additions.id: Smooth slimy honey-yellow caps with a darker center; narrow crowded gills mature brown and thin stems darken below.
additions.look: The spumosa group and other smooth yellow-brown Pholiota are close comparisons; deadly Galerina must also be excluded.
details: Caps are often 2–4 cm wide. A pale veil may leave remnants on the margin and scattered fibrils on the stem.
The original description emphasizes microscopic chrysocystidia and a combination of habitat and anatomy. Several Warren Woods specimens document the name locally.
additions.nativeStatus: Documented wild occurrence; these sources do not independently establish native-versus-introduced status.

additions.name: Pholiota parvifructa — historical record
additions.aliases: Hebeloma parvifructum, Agaricus parvifructus, Derminus parvifructus, Pholiota parvifructa
additions.months: September in the local historical collection; broader season unresolved here
additions.habitat: The local label says under hemlock (Tsuga) and other trees
additions.id: Included as a historical occurrence, with no validated field-identification description for the local specimen.
additions.look: A brown gilled mushroom cannot be assigned this name from the historic record or from a photograph. Expert specimen examination is needed.
details: The New Richmond specimen was filed under Hebeloma parvifructum. Species Fungorum recognizes the combination Pholiota parvifructa published in 2022.
That nomenclatural change does not re-identify the 1910 Michigan specimen. This entry preserves the record for completeness; it is not a field-identification key.

historicalNames.name: Pholiota aggericola
historicalNames.treatment: Held for taxonomic clarification: Smith & Hesler excluded it from Pholiota and discussed Agrocybe. Not counted as a confirmed current Pholiota.

historicalNames.name: Pholiota populnea
historicalNames.treatment: Now commonly treated as Hemipholiota populnea; former Pholiota, excluded from the current-genus count.

historicalNames.name: Pholiota tuberculosa / Pholiota curvipes
historicalNames.treatment: Now treated as Pleuroflammula tuberculosa in iNaturalist. Historical Warren Woods specimens were filed as P. curvipes; not counted as a current Pholiota.

historicalNames.name: Pholiota veris
historicalNames.treatment: Mapped to Kuehneromyces marginellus by iNaturalist; former Pholiota, excluded from the current-genus count.
